reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Occurs in residents of, or long-stay travellers to, endemic tropical regions and presents with chronic diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, weight loss and fatigue
Characteristically causes malabsorption of both folate and vitamin B12, producing a macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia
Unlike coeliac disease it involves the entire small bowel including the ileum, which explains the B12 deficiency
Diagnosis is one of exclusion, requiring documented malabsorption and villous changes on small-bowel biopsy after ruling out parasitic and other infective causes
Small-bowel histology shows partial villous atrophy with crypt changes, generally milder than the total atrophy of coeliac disease
Management combines antibiotic courses for bacterial overgrowth of the small bowel together with folate and vitamin B12 replacement
A history of residence in the tropics, sometimes months or years earlier, is a key diagnostic clue
reference.pathophysiology: Tropical sprue is an acquired malabsorptive disorder of the small intestine occurring in tropical regions, believed to follow an enteric infection that leads to persistent colonisation of the upper small bowel by abnormal coliform bacteria. This chronic overgrowth, together with resulting mucosal injury and impaired motility, damages the villi throughout the small intestine and impairs absorption of nutrients including folate and vitamin B12. Deficiency of these vitamins further impairs enterocyte turnover, perpetuating villous atrophy in a self-sustaining cycle until the abnormal flora and deficiencies are corrected.
additionalDifferentials: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth from other causes
HIV enteropathy and other immunodeficiency-related enteropathies
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film with folate and vitamin B12 levels to detect megaloblastic anaemia
Small-bowel biopsy showing partial villous atrophy
Stool microscopy and specific tests to exclude parasitic and other infections
Coeliac serology to exclude coeliac disease
Assessment of fat malabsorption and other nutritional deficiencies
redFlags: Profound weight loss and cachexia from prolonged malabsorption
Severe anaemia with symptoms from combined folate and B12 deficiency
Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance from persistent diarrhoea
Failure to respond to treatment, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: With appropriate antibiotic therapy and vitamin replacement the prognosis is generally excellent and relapse is uncommon once the patient has left the endemic area, though untreated disease can cause severe nutritional depletion.
pitfalls: Confusing it with coeliac disease and missing the ileal involvement and B12 deficiency
Failing to exclude parasitic infection before making the diagnosis
Overlooking a remote history of tropical residence
Neglecting to replace both folate and vitamin B12 alongside antibiotics
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Give a prolonged course of a tetracycline such as tetracycline or doxycycline to eradicate the abnormal small-bowel coliform overgrowth
Replace folate and vitamin B12 to correct the megaloblastic anaemia and support enterocyte recovery
Correct associated nutritional deficiencies and provide nutritional rehabilitation with fluid and electrolyte replacement
Advise that leaving the endemic area aids recovery and reduces relapse
Monitor symptoms, haematological indices and nutritional status to confirm response to treatment
Reassess the diagnosis, excluding coeliac disease and persistent parasitic infection, if there is no response
